Flooding in Central Chile Disrupts Hospitality Industry Operations

Severe flooding in central Chile has brought significant disruption to the country’s hospitality industry, as heavy rains continue to inundate hotels, resorts, and restaurants across the region. The event, which began late last week, has seen record rainfall swell rivers and overflow banks, submerging properties and forcing widespread closures.

According to the Chilean Hospitality Association, over 60% of member sites in the O’Higgins and Maule regions have experienced flooding of varying degrees. “We are witnessing one of the most challenging natural events in recent memory,” said Association President Gabriela Mena. “Many of our colleagues have seen their premises damaged, with some hotels reporting water levels reaching up to a metre in ground-floor areas.”

The effects on workers have been immediate. Hundreds of employees at affected establishments have been sent home or shifted to emergency maintenance tasks as management teams assess damage and attempt to safeguard facilities. “Our priority is the safety of our staff and guests,” stated Ignacio Rojas, general manager of the Gran Valle Hotel Group. “With guest rooms and kitchens inundated, we had no choice but to evacuate everyone and suspend operations.”

Estimates from industry analysts suggest that the cost of direct damage to hospitality premises could exceed $38 million if the flooding continues through the week. Many businesses are struggling to protect their properties, with sandbagging and water pumps proving insufficient in the face of persistent rainfall. “We are using every resource at our disposal, but the water keeps rising,” said Paula Troncoso, owner of the Arenas del Sur Lodge in Constitución.

Local hospitality unions have raised concerns for workers’ well-being, pointing to potential longer-term impacts. “Many employees rely on daily wages, and every day of closure represents a lost income,” said union leader Sergio Pizarro. “We urge companies to prioritize staff support during this crisis.”

As the flooding shows little sign of abating, industry leaders are calling for coordinated efforts to minimize further losses and plan for eventual recovery. “Once the rains subside, we will have to confront the full extent of the damage,” Mena said. “For now, our focus remains on weathering the immediate emergency and protecting our people and sites as best we can.”
